newsitem.title: THAILAND: Bundesbank reiterates dollar has risen enough.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank reiterates dollar has risen enough.

text.p: A top Bundesbank official reiterated on Thursday the German central bank's view the U.S. dollar had gone up far enough in the latest effort to stem the currency's inexorable rise.

"I once more underline, it is not in the interest of the Bundesbank that the strength of the dollar goes further and further," Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum told Reuters Financial Television.
"I think the message from the Berlin (G7) meeting...is no longer a situation of an overvalued mark," he added.
Gaddum's remarks helped push the dollar lower in Asia but foreign exchange dealers said they were still bullish on the currency.

His comments also came less than a day after the Bundesbank took the unusual step of denying -- through its chief spokesman -- a news agency report that Germany was keen to see the U.S. currency move still higher.
"The Bundesbank is definitely not of the opinion that the dollar should rise further," the chief spokesman said on Wednesday.
Last weekend's Group of Seven (G7) meeting ended with the members -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, the United States and Japan -- issuing a brief communique concerning the dollar.

"We believe that major misalignments in exchange markets...have been corrected. We reaffirmed our views that exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals and that excess volatility is undesirable," the statement said.

Gaddum, attending a regional central bankers meeting in Bangkok, said he believed that the G7 consensus on the dollar remained intact and added that the Bundesbank was not looking for a specific level for the mark.
The dollar has risen some 15 percent against the mark since last August and has soared even more against the Japanese yen.
At 0700 GMT, the mark was quoted at 1.6805/12 marks, compared with Wednesday's close of 1.6890/95.
However, despite the Bundesbank's desire to keep the dollar from rising further, foreign exchange dealers said they expect the currency to move higher in the short term.

A dollar trader at a bank in Singapore noted that Thursday's remarks by Gaddum had merely caused the dollar to dip back on profit-taking. "Every time it backtracks, it finds a new base from which to go higher," he said.
He added that to stop the dollar's rise, the G7 central banks would have to intervene massively. "They've not shown any inclination to do that," he said.
The head of foreign exchange trading at a European bank in Singapore commented, "The G7 statement told us to look at fundamentals. Well I am and the fundamentals say 'buy the dollar, sell the mark'."

"The U.S. has low inflation, an unemployment rate the envy of the rest of the world and the Dow (Jones Index) is about to go through 7,000. The fundamentals are absolutely bloody marvellous," he added.
